title: DOM Manipulation
subtitle: How Your Dashboard Creates Cards, Updates XP, Progress Bar and Makes It Interactive
description: Master DOM - getElementById, querySelector, createElement, innerHTML vs textContent (XSS security), appendChild, style, classList, attributes, events, reflow performance, accessibility - everything pro must know, based on your dashboard's exact DOM code.

blocks.text: PAGE 1: What is DOM? Your Dashboard's HTML as Tree Your JS Controls

Hey friend! DOM = Document Object Model - browser turns your HTML into tree of objects that JavaScript can control. Your HTML
...
0 XP
...
becomes tree: document -> html -> body -> nav.navbar -> div.nav-right -> div.stat-pill -> span#xpValue. JavaScript can find, create, modify, delete nodes in this tree.

Your dashboard's JavaScript does: document.getElementById('xpValue') finds span with id xpValue, document.getElementById('lessonContainer') finds div for lessons, document.createElement('article') creates new card element, card.innerHTML = `...` sets HTML inside card, grid.appendChild(card) adds card to grid, lessonContainer.appendChild(grid) adds grid to container, xpValue.textContent = '120 XP' updates text, progressFill.style.width = '20%' updates style.

Without DOM manipulation, your dashboard would be static HTML - no dynamic XP, no progress bar moving, no lesson cards from Firebase, no loading spinner. DOM manipulation makes HTML alive - JavaScript reads and writes HTML tree.

Good programmer must know: DOM is slow - each appendChild, style change can cause reflow (browser recalculates layout) - 10 appends = 10 reflows slow. Your dashboard builds grid in memory then appends once = 1 reflow fast. Also security: innerHTML with user data can cause XSS attack - if lesson title is '<script>alert('hacked')</script>' and you do innerHTML = title, script executes! Use textContent for user data, not innerHTML.

Also accessibility: button with disabled attribute and aria-label, keyboard navigation, semantic article tag for lesson card not just div. Your dashboard uses article for lesson card - semantic HTML good for screen readers. Pro programmers care about performance, security, accessibility, not just working.

blocks.text: PAGE 2: Finding Elements - getElementById, querySelector, querySelectorAll

Finding elements: getElementById('xpValue') finds by id - fastest, returns one element or null. Your dashboard uses this for all 6 elements because they have ids. querySelector('.lesson-card') finds first element matching CSS selector - class, tag, attribute. querySelectorAll('.lesson-card') finds all matching - returns NodeList array-like.

Your dashboard: document.getElementById('lessonContainer') - by id, unique. Could also use document.querySelector('#lessonContainer') - # for id,. for class. querySelector('#xpValue') same as getElementById('xpValue') but slower. For class: document.querySelector('.lesson-card') first card, document.querySelectorAll('.lesson-card') all cards.

Good programmer: Use getElementById for id - fastest. Use querySelector for complex selectors: document.querySelector('.lesson-card:not(.locked).start-btn') - first start button in non-locked card. Use querySelectorAll for multiple elements then forEach to loop.

Null check important: If you do document.getElementById('xpValue') but element doesn't exist, returns null, then null.textContent throws TypeError: Cannot read property textContent of null. Your dashboard's script at bottom ensures HTML loaded before finding elements, so not null. Or check if (xpValue) { xpValue.textContent =... } safe.

Creating: document.createElement('article') creates new element, not yet in DOM, in memory. Your dashboard: const card = document.createElement('article'); card.className = `lesson-card ${isLocked? 'locked' : ''}`; sets class. Then card.innerHTML = `...` sets HTML inside card with template literal containing lesson title, learn, summary, badge, button.
Modifying: element.textContent = 'text' sets text, safe, no HTML parsing, prevents XSS. element.innerHTML = 'text' sets HTML, parses HTML, can have XSS if user data contains

element.style.width = '20%' sets inline style, element.style.background = 'red'. Your dashboard: progressFill.style.width = `${percent}%` sets progress bar width. element.className = 'lesson-card locked' sets class, element.classList.add('locked') adds class, classList.remove('locked') removes, classList.toggle('locked') toggles.

Good programmer: Use textContent for user data to prevent XSS, use innerHTML only for trusted HTML templates like your card template with static structure. Use classList for classes not className overwriting. Use createElement + appendChild for dynamic elements.

blocks.text: PAGE 4: innerHTML vs textContent - XSS Security Every Pro Must Know

innerHTML sets HTML and parses it - browser creates elements from HTML string. textContent sets text only - no HTML parsing, escapes < > as text. Security: If user input is '<script>alert(document.cookie)</script>' and you do element.innerHTML = userInput, browser executes script, steals cookies, XSS attack! If you do element.textContent = userInput, browser shows '<script>alert...</script>' as text, not executed, safe.

Your dashboard: lesson titles from static array ['Introduction to JavaScript', 'Variables',...] trusted, not user input, so innerHTML safe for card template. But if you had user comments or lesson titles from Firebase user input, you must use textContent for title, not innerHTML, or sanitize input.

Good programmer: Use textContent for any user-generated data: usernames, comments, titles from database, search input. Use innerHTML only for trusted HTML templates you control, like your card structure with divs, spans, classes - not for data inside. Or use createElement + textContent for each part: const h3 = createElement('h3'); h3.textContent = lesson.title; card.appendChild(h3); - safest, no innerHTML, no XSS, but more code.

Your dashboard uses innerHTML for card because it has complex HTML with many divs, badges, buttons - creating each with createElement would be 20 lines vs 1 template literal with innerHTML. For static trusted data, innerHTML okay and faster to code. For user data, textContent safer.

blocks.text: PAGE 5: Appending and Performance - Your Dashboard's Efficient Grid

Appending: parent.appendChild(child) adds child to parent in DOM, visible on page. Your dashboard: grid.appendChild(card) adds card to grid div, lessonContainer.appendChild(grid) adds grid to container. Append is expensive - causes reflow (browser recalculates layout, positions, sizes).

Performance: If you do forEach lesson => container.appendChild(card) directly inside loop, 10 lessons = 10 appends = 10 reflows, browser recalculates layout 10 times, slow. Your dashboard does: create grid div, forEach append cards to grid (grid not yet in DOM, in memory, no reflow), then container.appendChild(grid) once = 1 reflow, 10x faster! Build in memory then append once is pro pattern.
Also innerHTML = '' clears container: lessonContainer.innerHTML = '' removes all children quickly. Your dashboard does this before rendering to clear old cards and loading spinner.

Good programmer: Minimize DOM operations, batch appends, build in memory then append once, cache elements (const xpValue = getElementById, reuse, not getElementById every time), use DocumentFragment for many appends: fragment = createDocumentFragment(), forEach card => fragment.appendChild(card), container.appendChild(fragment) - 1 reflow.

blocks.question: Q2: You have 10 lessons, you do container.appendChild(card) directly inside forEach loop vs grid method: create grid, forEach grid.appendChild(card), container.appendChild(grid). First causes 10 reflows, second 1 reflow. Why and which your dashboard uses? Performance critical!
options: Direct append in loop triggers browser reflow (layout recalc) for each append - 10 cards 10 reflows slow. Grid method builds cards in memory grid not in DOM, no reflow, then appends grid once 1 reflow fast, 10x faster! Your dashboard uses grid method - createElement grid, append cards to grid in memory, append grid to container once - efficient pro pattern
blocks.correctFeedback: Exactly! 1 reflow vs 10 reflows - 10x faster! Build in memory then append once efficient. Your dashboard's grid method is pro performance pattern!
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Direct append in loop: Each appendChild triggers reflow - browser recalculates layout, 10 times slow. Grid method: Append to grid in memory not in DOM no reflow, then append grid to container once 1 reflow fast. Your dashboard: grid = createElement('div'), forEach grid.appendChild(card), container.appendChild(grid) - 1 reflow efficient.
blocks.reasoning: Reflow performance - building in memory then single append 1 reflow vs direct append many reflows.

blocks.text: PAGE 6: Style, ClassList, Attributes - Your Dashboard's Progress Bar and Badges

Style: element.style.width = '20%' sets inline style, element.style.background = 'linear-gradient(...)' sets background. Your dashboard: progressFill.style.width = `${percent}%` sets progress bar width dynamically, card.style.background for glassmorphism, badge.style.color for status colors.

ClassList: element.classList.add('locked') adds class, remove('locked') removes, toggle('locked') adds if not exists removes if exists, contains('locked') checks if has class. Your dashboard: card.className = `lesson-card ${isLocked? 'locked' : ''}` sets class, could use classList.add('locked') if locked.

Attributes: element.setAttribute('data-lesson', lesson.id) sets attribute, getAttribute('data-lesson') gets, element.dataset.lesson = lesson.id sets data attribute. Your dashboard: button data-lesson attribute to store lesson id, then button.dataset.lesson to get id in click handler.

Good programmer: Use classList for classes not className overwriting, use dataset for data attributes, use style for dynamic styles like width, but prefer CSS classes for static styles. Your dashboard uses className for card, style.width for progress dynamic.

blocks.text: PAGE 7: Events - Your Dashboard's Click Handlers

Events: User actions like click, mouseover, keydown, load. addEventListener('click', callback) listens for click event and calls callback when clicked. Your dashboard: backBtn.addEventListener('click', () => { if (referrer && includes) history.back() else menu.html }) - when back button clicked, callback navigates. button.addEventListener('click', () => { window.location.href = lesson.html }) - when Start Lesson clicked, navigate to lesson.

Event object: callback receives event object with details: event.target is element clicked, event.preventDefault() prevents default behavior like form submit reload. Your dashboard's back button doesn't need preventDefault because button not in form, but form submit would need preventDefault.

Good programmer: Use addEventListener not onclick attribute - addEventListener allows multiple listeners, onclick overwrites. Use event delegation for many buttons: Instead of adding listener to each of 10 Start buttons, add one listener to grid parent and check event.target if button - more efficient, works for dynamically added cards.

blocks.question: Q3: You have 10 Start Lesson buttons, you addEventListener click to each button - 10 listeners. Alternative: Add one listener to grid parent and check event.target if button - delegation. Which better for performance and dynamic cards? Pro must know!
options: Delegation better - one listener on parent grid, not 10 listeners, less memory, faster, and works for dynamically added cards after initial render - new cards added later automatically handled by parent listener, no need to add listener to each new card. Your dashboard adds listener to each button, works but delegation more efficient for many buttons and dynamic content
blocks.correctFeedback: Exactly! Delegation one listener efficient, handles dynamic cards, less memory. Pro pattern for many buttons!
blocks.incorrectFeedback: 10 listeners - 10 functions in memory, add listener to each new card. Delegation - 1 listener on parent grid, checks event.target, 1 function, less memory, faster, works for dynamically added cards automatically - new cards no need new listener, parent handles. Pro pattern!
blocks.reasoning: Event delegation - one parent listener vs many child listeners - efficient and handles dynamic content.

blocks.text: PAGE 10: Summary & Tricky Final Questions - Pro Must Know

You mastered DOM pro level: Finding getElementById fastest for id, querySelector for CSS, querySelectorAll all matching, null check if element exists. Creating createElement, modifying textContent safe for user data prevents XSS, innerHTML parses HTML dangerous for user input but okay for trusted templates like your card structure. Appending appendChild causes reflow, build in memory grid then append once 1 reflow 10x faster than direct append in loop 10 reflows - your dashboard uses efficient grid method. DocumentFragment even better for many elements.

blocks.question: Q7: You do document.getElementById('xpValue') but element doesn't exist - returns null, then null.textContent throws TypeError. How to prevent and why your dashboard script at bottom prevents null? Good programmer null check!

Alternative: DOMContentLoaded event or defer or type=module waits for HTML. Good programmer always null checks or ensures script after HTML
